label: Geodesics and Distance
notes: This chapter, printed pages 151 to 192, turns the abstract Levi-Civita connection into geometry you can walk along. We trace a single thread: curves of zero acceleration, the exponential map that emits them, and how they govern shortest paths and the Riemannian distance between points.

label: Geodesics as Zero Acceleration
notes: A geodesic is the connection's notion of a straight line: its velocity is parallel along itself, so covariant acceleration vanishes. Because the Levi-Civita connection is built from the metric, this single condition encodes everything the metric knows about going straight, independent of any chart.

label: The Geodesic Equation
notes: In coordinates the covariant condition becomes a coupled system of second-order ordinary differential equations driven by the Christoffel symbols. Existence and uniqueness for such systems guarantees exactly one maximal geodesic through each point in each direction, the fact that underwrites every later construction.

label: The Exponential Map
notes: Following the unique geodesic with a given initial velocity for unit time defines the exponential map from the tangent space into the manifold. It packages all geodesics through one point into a single smooth map and is the workhorse for transferring linear structure to the curved space.

label: Normal Neighborhoods
notes: Because the exponential map has invertible differential at the origin, it is a diffeomorphism on a small star-shaped ball. Its image is a normal neighborhood in which every point is joined to the center by a unique radial geodesic, giving us privileged coordinates centered at that point.

label: Normal and Geodesic Coordinates
notes: Pulling back through the exponential map yields normal coordinates in which geodesics through the origin are straight lines, the metric is the identity there, and Christoffel symbols vanish at the center. These coordinates dramatically simplify local computations and proofs about curvature.

label: The Gauss Lemma
notes: The Gauss lemma states that radial geodesics from the center meet the geodesic spheres around it orthogonally. This orthogonality is the geometric heart of why radial geodesics are efficient, and it converts metric questions near a point into clean statements about radius and angle.

label: Riemannian Distance
notes: The Riemannian distance between two points is the infimum of lengths of admissible curves joining them. This turns a connected Riemannian manifold into a genuine metric space whose topology agrees with the manifold topology, linking smooth geometry to the language of analysis.

label: Geodesics Locally Minimize
notes: Using the Gauss lemma we show that inside a normal ball the radial geodesic is strictly shorter than any other curve to the same point. So geodesics are locally length-minimizing, although globally a geodesic may overshoot the true shortest route, as on a sphere.

label: Minimizing vs Competitor
notes: We compare the radial geodesic against a longer competitor curve between the same endpoints. Decomposing the competitor's velocity into radial and spherical parts and applying the Gauss lemma shows only the radial part contributes the minimum length, so any detour strictly costs extra arc length.

label: Geodesic Completeness
notes: A manifold is geodesically complete when every maximal geodesic extends to all real time, so the exponential map is defined on the whole tangent space. Completeness is exactly the condition preventing geodesics from running off an edge or into a puncture in finite time.

label: The Hopf-Rinow Theorem
notes: Hopf and Rinow prove that geodesic completeness, metric completeness, and the Heine-Borel property all coincide for a connected Riemannian manifold. Crucially, any one of them guarantees that every pair of points is joined by a globally minimizing geodesic, closing the loop between connection and distance.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: From zero acceleration we built the exponential map, normal coordinates, and the Gauss lemma, then proved geodesics minimize locally and, under completeness, globally. The Riemannian distance and Hopf-Rinow unify these threads, equipping later chapters on Jacobi fields and comparison theory with a rigorous foundation.
